short_description: PCOS is a common hormone pattern that can make periods less regular.
what_happens_inside_my_body: The ovaries make hormones and usually release an egg in a cycle.
With PCOS, that signalling can shift, so egg release becomes less regular.
The body may make more hormones called androgens, which can show up as acne or extra hair growth.
Some people also become less sensitive to insulin, the hormone that helps sugar move into cells. Not everyone with PCOS has this.
why_it_matters: Less regular periods, skin changes and trouble getting pregnant are reasons people look into PCOS.
Over time it can sit alongside higher blood sugar, cholesterol changes and a higher chance of diabetes or heart risk.
A Bio-AI PCOS score is a predicted risk, not a diagnosis. A doctor uses symptoms, an exam and tests together.
relevant_lifestyle_factors: Moving more often and including vegetables, pulses, fruit and unsweetened drinks can support insulin sensitivity.
Sleep and stress matter for hormones, but a habit does not by itself cause a PCOS score.
Weight can be associated with PCOS. It is not the cause for everyone, and a prediction does not say a person's eating caused it.
common_misconceptions: A predicted risk does not mean you have PCOS.
PCOS and PCOD are names for the same conversation here, not two separate conditions.
No single blood test confirms PCOS, and a missing assessment does not mean there is no risk.
PCOS is not caused by one food, and it is not only a weight problem.
clinical_limitations: Diagnosis needs a clinician. Irregular periods, androgen signs and ultrasound findings are weighed together.
This library does not set a score cutoff, and it does not say which inputs produced a member's score.
Medicines, supplements and doses are a doctor's decision, not something this explanation can set.

short_description: Oxidative stress is what happens when substances your cells make as they work build up faster than your body's protective systems can handle them.
what_happens_inside_my_body: Your cells naturally make some reactive molecules as they use energy.
Your body has protective systems that help keep these molecules in balance.
When that protection cannot keep up, the extra molecules may damage parts of cells. That imbalance is called oxidative stress.
why_it_matters: Over time, this imbalance can affect the health of cells.
Research discusses oxidative stress alongside inflammation and some longer-term health conditions. A score does not show that this has happened.
Everyday habits such as smoking, eating patterns, sleep and physical activity are studied as general influences. They are not confirmed reasons for an individual score.
everyday_support: Include a variety of vegetables, fruit, pulses and other minimally processed foods.
Keep a sleep routine that gives you enough rest.
Stay physically active in a way that fits your usual day.
common_misconceptions: A normal blood test in this area does not cancel a higher predicted oxidative stress risk, because routine blood tests do not directly measure it.
clinical_limitations: This score is a risk estimate, not a direct measurement of cell damage and not a diagnosis. A number out of 100 is the provider's score, not a percentage chance.

short_description: Metabolic age is an estimate that compares parts of metabolic health with age-related patterns.
product_inputs: MetSights can look at blood biomarkers, lifestyle, food, activity, sleep, demographics and other questionnaire answers when it builds risk scores and metabolic scores.
That is the known general input set. The formula, feature weights and reference population are not available, and not every answer feeds every score.
what_happens_inside_my_body: The body turns food into energy, keeps blood sugar in a workable range and handles fats through the day. That is metabolic health. It is not how quickly someone burns calories or loses weight.
Your actual age is how many years you have lived. Metabolic age is a Bio-AI estimate related to those processes, not a count of birthdays and not biological age.
A higher, lower or matching estimate is a way to look at metabolic health. It does not measure lifespan and it is not a diagnosis.
Favourable blood results and a higher estimate can exist together, because a prediction is not the same thing as a measurement.
A later assessment can show a different number. No habit is promised to move it by a set number of years.
why_it_matters: A higher, lower or matching estimate is a starting point for looking at metabolic health, not a judgement of how well someone is ageing.
It does not measure remaining lifespan, and it does not mean the whole body is that many years older or younger.
relevant_lifestyle_factors: Everyday movement, meals built around vegetables, pulses and unsweetened drinks, and regular sleep support metabolic health.
Those habits are discussed separately from the estimate unless a documented method says they contributed to it.
common_misconceptions: A higher metabolic age does not mean accelerated ageing or lost years of life.
A lower metabolic age does not guarantee good health.
A normal blood result can exist alongside a higher estimate.
Lifestyle changes are not guaranteed to move the number by a set number of years.
clinical_limitations: This is not a diagnosis.
The provider field is a reported estimate. The calculation method and model attribution are not in the supplied assessment schema.
Do not treat a missing estimate as normal health.
